task: Describe en 80–100 palabras una tradición de tu país: origen, qué se hace hoy y qué opinas.
paragraphs: If you are in Britain on the evening of 5 November, you will probably hear loud bangs and see the sky full of colourful fireworks. It is Bonfire Night, also called Guy Fawkes Night, one of the most popular traditions in the country.

The story goes back to 1605. A group of Catholic men, unhappy with the way they were treated by the Protestant king, James I, planned to blow up the Houses of Parliament in London while the king was inside. One of them, Guy Fawkes, was found guarding barrels of gunpowder in a cellar under the building on the night of 4 November. The plot, known as the Gunpowder Plot, failed, and the men involved were arrested and executed.

To celebrate the king's survival, people lit bonfires around London, and the tradition continued. For centuries, children made a "guy", a figure of Guy Fawkes made of old clothes stuffed with newspaper, and asked passers-by for "a penny for the guy". The figure was then burned on the bonfire. Today this custom is much less common.

Modern Bonfire Night is mostly about having fun. Towns organise public firework displays, and families gather around bonfires with hot drinks, toffee apples and sausages. A famous rhyme begins, "Remember, remember the fifth of November, gunpowder, treason and plot."

Not everyone loves the celebration, though. Fireworks can frighten pets and wildlife, and every year doctors treat injuries caused by them. That is why many people prefer to go to organised events rather than set off fireworks at home.
